lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- The Decision Memo
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Cassio Haunholter Xavier da Silva | Lesson 10 -- The Decision Memo
lesson.grammar_point: modals of certainty and hedging language

listenings.text: I sign off decisions I am not qualified to make technically, which is an uncomfortable thing to say out loud, and it is the job. So what I am really judging is not the engineering, it is whether the person writing has shown me the edge of what they know. The memos that worry me are the confident ones with no caveats. Nothing in a project is that certain, so either the writer has not looked hard enough, or they have looked and decided not to tell me, and I cannot tell which from the page. When I get one of those, I ask one question in the meeting: what would have to be true for this to be wrong? A good engineer answers that in about ten seconds, because they have already asked themselves. And the answer is usually the caveat that should have been in the memo, so we put it in, and then I sign.

Eighteen months ago I wrote that a solution would work. Not was likely to work. Would. I believed it, and I was about eighty per cent right, which is normally fine. The twenty per cent was a ground condition in one corner of the site, and it cost six weeks and a lot of money. Nobody blamed me for the ground. What they remembered was the sentence. Since then I have had to earn back something I did not know I had, which is the weight my writing used to carry. It is a strange thing to lose. Now I write likely, and I write the condition, and once or twice somebody has asked me whether I am being evasive. I tell them the truth: I am being exact. If I write that something will happen, I mean it, and now that means something again. The honest hedge is not weaker than the promise. It is the only version you can repeat for twenty years.

reading.rtitle: What a Good Memo Puts First
paras: A decision memo exists for one reason: somebody has to choose, and they are not going to read five pages to do it. So the recommendation goes in the first line, not at the end after the analysis. Engineers resist this, because the reasoning feels like the work and the conclusion feels like an opinion. But a reader who does not know where you are going cannot follow why you are going there, and by page two they have decided for themselves.

After the recommendation comes the rationale, and a good rationale is short: the criteria you used, the option you ruled out and why. Then the two lists that most memos leave out. The assumptions, which are the things you have treated as true without proving them, and the constraints, which are the limits you had no power over. These two are not the same, and mixing them is how a memo becomes hard to challenge. An assumption can be tested. A constraint cannot, and pretending otherwise wastes everybody’s time.

The last thing is the caveats, and this is where the language matters most. A memo that says option A will work is believed once. A memo that says option A is likely to work, provided the soil report confirms the bearing capacity, and may require a thicker slab in the equipment area, is believed every time, because the reader can see the edge of what you know. Confidence in engineering is not the absence of doubt. It is doubt that has been measured and placed where the reader can find it.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A memo should present the full analysis first, so the reader can reach the conclusion alone.
A memo leads with the recommendation, separates assumptions from constraints, and states its caveats, because measured doubt is what makes it trusted.
A memo should avoid caveats, because they make the writer look uncertain.
